Quick answer: Arthritis medications include painkillers like paracetamol and stronger opioids for severe pain. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce both pain and inflammation. DMARDs and biologics treat underlying disease processes in inflammatory arthritis. Corticosteroids offer potent anti-inflammatory effects. Topical gels and creams can provide localised relief. Most are available on NHS prescription.

Taking medication for arthritis can feel like navigating a maze. There are so many names, so many warnings — and you just want something that helps.

This guide explains every major type of arthritis medication in plain English. We cover what each one does, how it works, potential side effects, and how to get it on the NHS. Always speak to your GP or rheumatologist before starting or stopping any medication.

Painkillers (Paracetamol, Codeine) for Arthritis

Paracetamol

Paracetamol is often the first painkiller your GP will suggest. It helps with mild-to-moderate pain and is generally safe when taken at the recommended dose (no more than 4g, or eight 500mg tablets, in 24 hours). Widely available, few side effects, inexpensive — but it does not reduce inflammation and may not be strong enough for severe pain.

Codeine and Other Opioids

Codeine, tramadol, and morphine-based drugs are stronger painkillers sometimes prescribed for short periods when pain is severe. Important warning: These medicines can cause dependence. The NHS recommends using the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. Common side effects include constipation, drowsiness, and nausea.

NSAIDs — Ibuprofen, Naproxen, and Cox-2 Inhibitors

NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) relieve both pain and inflammation. They are widely used for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other types.

  • Traditional NSAIDs: Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Diclofenac — available over the counter or on prescription.
  • Cox-2 inhibitors: Celecoxib, Etoricoxib — prescription-only; may be gentler on the stomach.

Potential side effects: NSAIDs can irritate the stomach lining. Your GP may prescribe a stomach-protecting drug (proton pump inhibitor, or PPI) alongside them. Long-term use at high doses may affect kidney function or blood pressure. People with asthma, stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or heart conditions should speak to their GP before taking NSAIDs.

DMARDs for Inflammatory Arthritis

DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs) treat the underlying disease process in rheumatoid arthritis — they aim to slow or stop the immune system from attacking the joints. Common DMARDs include:

  • Methotrexate — Usually the first DMARD prescribed for RA. Taken once a week (not daily). Regular blood tests needed.
  • Sulfasalazine — Often used when methotrexate is not suitable or in combination with it.
  • Leflunomide — Another alternative or add-on DMARD.
  • Hydroxychloroquine — Milder DMARD, sometimes used for milder RA or lupus.

Key facts: They take 6–12 weeks to work. Regular blood monitoring is essential. They can affect the immune system, increasing infection risk. Stopping suddenly can cause a flare-up.

Biologics — Newer Treatments for RA

Biologics are a newer class of DMARD, made from living cells. They target very specific parts of the immune system involved in inflammation. Examples include Adalimumab (Humira), Etanercept (Enbrel), Infliximab (Remicade), and Tocilizumab (RoActemra). On the NHS, they are usually offered to people whose RA has not responded well to at least two standard DMARDs and whose disease activity remains high. They are given by injection or infusion and require careful monitoring.

Corticosteroid Injections and Tablets

Corticosteroids (often simply called "steroids") are powerful anti-inflammatories — not the same as anabolic steroids misused in sport. Steroid injections delivered directly into a painful joint can provide rapid relief lasting weeks to months (limit of 3–4 per year in the same joint). Steroid tablets (prednisolone) are used for short courses during severe flares or low-dose long-term control, though long-term use carries risks including weight gain, osteoporosis, and high blood pressure.

Topical Treatments (Gels and Creams)

Topical NSAIDs — ibuprofen gel or diclofenac gel — are applied directly to the skin over a painful joint. They cause fewer stomach side effects than tablets, deliver medication exactly where needed, and are available over the counter. Topical capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) works by reducing substance P, a chemical that sends pain signals — it can take a few weeks of regular use to show benefit.

Getting Arthritis Medication on the NHS

Most arthritis medications are available on NHS prescription. Over-the-counter drugs (paracetamol, ibuprofen gel, low-dose ibuprofen tablets) can be bought yourself — buying paracetamol in bulk is often cheaper than a prescription. Prescription NSAIDs, DMARDs, biologics, and steroids are prescribed by your GP or rheumatologist at the standard NHS prescription charge (£9.90 per item as of 2024/25), unless you qualify for free prescriptions. If you need regular medication, a Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC) costs around £32 for three months of unlimited prescriptions.

Talking to Your GP About Medication

  1. Be specific about your pain. "I struggle to open jars and my hands hurt every morning for an hour" is more helpful than "I'm in pain."
  2. Mention what you have already tried. Include exercise, over-the-counter medication, and lifestyle changes.
  3. Ask questions. Write them down beforehand.
  4. Discuss side effects openly. If a medicine makes you feel unwell, say so. There are usually alternatives.
  5. Do not stop medication suddenly. Some drugs (especially steroids) need to be reduced gradually under medical supervision.

Practical next steps for Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect

If you came here about Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Arthritis Medication What Works

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
